title: Three-Zone Post-Processing Workflow for Canadian Rockies Landscapes (Part 1)

date.basis: embedded_creation_time metadata indicates 2022-01-20; transcript indicates this is Part 1 of a multi-video series focused on Canadian Rockies images (Part 2 folder path suggests 2020-2022 timeline)

summary: This video presents a practical, multi-zone workflow for editing Canadian Rockies landscape images in Photoshop, emphasizing perceptual dynamic range, per-zone adjustments, and iterative layering. The presenter demonstrates flattening a wide scene to a true-to-eye dynamic range, then treating foreground, mid-ground, and sky as separate zones to be adjusted with Camera Raw, the history brush, and targeted masking. The tutorial covers sky enhancements via whites, warmth, dehaze, color grading, and camera calibration, followed by careful sky replacement and perspective adjustments (including the rule of trapezoids and perspective warp). The narrator also discusses atmospheric rendering, depth via blur, selective light painting (including highlight dodge cautions), and the constant trade-off between global edits and localized refinements, interspersed with on-screen troubleshooting and reflections on workflow pace. The sequence culminates in a directional-light emphasis on the left side and a reminder that future videos will continue with Castle Mountain shots in the same processing framework.

sections.title: Intro and workflow framing
sections.description: The presenter introduces the session’s goal: review a variety of Canadian Rockies images and explain the process. He emphasizes that approximately 90% of processing is done in post and only about 10% is decision-making on-site, with adjustments to start big and refine over time.

sections.title: Zone concept and composition decisions
sections.description: The video explains identifying how many zones (foreground, middle ground, sky) exist in a shot and why it's important to keep the peak fully in frame and to leave more space where light originates.

sections.title: Dynamic range flattening to match eye perception
sections.description: The first processing pass aims to approximate what the eye sees by expanding the dynamic range so shadows remain visible and nothing in the sky or foreground is blown out. The presenter notes that starting with a dim, multi-zone frame preserves room to shape light later.

sections.title: Per-zone RAW edits and history-brush technique
sections.description: The workflow returns to RAW to rework each zone separately. The foreground is brightened for texture, the middle ground kept simple, and a sky adjustment is prepared. The history brush is used to erase or reapply adjustments, simulating layer-like control without traditional layers.

sections.title: Sky adjustments: exposure, warmth, and color grading
sections.description: Sky adjustments begin with reducing exposure and restoring whites to reveal drama, then balancing warmth. A color grading step targets highlight colors, followed by camera calibration tweaks to balance blue tones in the ice.

sections.title: Multi-pass sky coloration and masking
sections.description: A second sky pass uses tonal-based adjustments to preserve control over color while preventing color bleed. The sky is split into zones for precise enhancement, with painting via history brush to apply changes only where intended.

sections.title: Sky integration and edge refinement (two-sky approach)
sections.description: The instructor details blending a new sky into the shot, including warping and trapezoid adjustments to fit a wide-angle composition. Edges are refined with hard and soft brushes, clone stamping, and careful cropping to maintain continuity between sky and mountains.

sections.title: Detailed edge work and sky-edge continuity
sections.description: Continuing sky replacement with precise edge work, the presenter demonstrates aligning cloud patterns and ensuring consistent transitions at the sky/mountain boundary, including selective cloning and perspective tweaks.

sections.title: Atmosphere and depth via blur and glow
sections.description: Atmospheric rendering is introduced to create separation between background and foreground. Blur is applied to background, with tweaks to shadows and highlights to preserve depth and a believable glow.

sections.title: Directional light shaping and final polish
sections.description: A strong left-side directional light is painted into the scene to add three-dimensionality. The speaker discusses selective use of highlight dodge to warm highlights, cautions about blue colors, and refining shadows to maintain color integrity.

sections.title: Wrap and preview of next steps
sections.description: The video closes with a note that subsequent shots in the Castle Mountain segment will follow the same processing approach, suggesting continuity in the series.
